question:
Patient note:
A 63-year-old man with a fifteen-year history of alcohol-associated cirrhosis—last drink six weeks earlier after enrolling in an outpatient rehabilitation program—walked into the emergency department late this afternoon because over the prior five days his belt no longer reached the third hole, he struggled to bend forward to tie his shoes, and he noted progressive abdominal pressure that forced him to sleep propped on two pillows; he denied confusion, changes in sleep–wake cycle, tremor, personality shifts, or episodes of staring, and he continued to balance his checkbook and complete the daily newspaper crossword without difficulty. Past medical history includes remote chronic hepatitis C successfully treated with ledipasvir/sofosbuvir five years ago, staple line hernia repair following Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, and stage 3 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine of 1.4 mg/dL. He takes furosemide 40 mg and spironolactone 100 mg each morning, propranolol 20 mg twice daily for portal pressure reduction, and thiamine 100 mg daily; he has no drug allergies. He smokes half a pack of cigarettes per day, quit intravenous drug use two decades ago, and lives alone in a single-story apartment. Family history is significant for a brother who died of esophageal variceal hemorrhage at 58 and a father with myocardial infarction at 60. Review of systems is otherwise negative for fever, chills, jaundice noted by friends, hematemesis, melena, hematochezia, pruritus, shortness of breath at rest, chest pain, palpitations, or recent medication changes. On arrival—before intravenous access, diagnostic paracentesis, diuretics, vitamin K, antibiotics, albumin, or any sedative—vital signs were temperature 36.9 °C, blood pressure 102/60 mm Hg, heart rate 96 beats/min in regular rhythm, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 96 % on ambient air. He was alert, maintained eye contact, recalled three objects after five minutes, spelled the word “world” backward quickly, and held his arms outstretched for twenty seconds without a flapping motion. Sclerae carried a deep yellow tint, conjunctivae were anemic, and the breath emitted a faint odor of stale beer. Dozens of spider angiomata peppered the upper chest and shoulders, palmar erythema was pronounced, and nail beds were pale. Neck veins were flat at 30°. Cardiac examination demonstrated a tachy-but-regular rhythm without murmurs or extra sounds; lungs were clear to auscultation throughout. The abdomen ballooned into a smooth hemisphere with everted umbilicus; percussion revealed tympany centrally that shifted to broad flank dullness when he rolled, and a fluid impulse traversed the abdominal wall without the need for a second examiner’s counter-pressure, though the wall was still soft and not rock-hard. A firm, nodular liver edge was just palpable two centimeters below the right costal margin on deep inspiration, and the spleen was appreciated three fingerbreadths below the left costal margin. There was bilateral 1+ pitting edema to the mid-shins. Neurologic examination showed intact cranial nerves, symmetric 5/5 strength, normal tone, and a narrow-based gait down the corridor. Capillary glucose measured 102 mg/dL. Point-of-care abdominal ultrasonography performed at the bedside prior to phlebotomy demonstrated a shrunken, coarse, nodular liver, patent main portal vein with antegrade flow at 12 cm/s, spleen measuring 18 cm, and a freely mobile anechoic collection layering 6 cm deep in the right paracolic gutter and tracking into the pelvis; no focal hepatic masses or biliary dilation were seen. Laboratory studies drawn at that moment—before any therapeutic intervention—revealed total bilirubin 5.6 mg/dL, serum albumin 2.45 g/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 88 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 54 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 262 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 384 U/L, sodium 129 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 97 mmol/L, bicarbonate 20 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 38 mg/dL, creatinine 1.68 mg/dL, hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL, white blood cell count 7.6 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 68 × 10⁹/L, and a prothrombin time corresponding to an international normalized ratio of 2.06. Serum ammonia, blood cultures, and diagnostic ascitic fluid studies were sent but results were pending. A 12-lead electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus tachycardia at 98 beats/min with a QTc of 444 ms, and an upright chest radiograph revealed elevated hemidiaphragms with basilar atelectasis but no effusion. At this juncture no intravascular fluids, albumin infusions, antibiotics, diuretic adjustments, or procedural interventions had yet been initiated, so the findings above reflect his untreated physiologic status at presentation.

Question: What is the patient's Child-Pugh Score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Child-Pugh score assigns 1–3 points each for bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy. Use the admission findings before treatment:
- Total bilirubin 5.6 mg/dL (>3): 3 points.
- Albumin 2.45 g/dL (<2.8): 3 points.
- INR 2.06 (1.7–2.3): 2 points.
- Ascites: marked symptomatic distention, shifting dullness, and a fluid wave despite outpatient diuretics indicate moderate-to-severe ascites: 3 points.
- Encephalopathy: alert with intact attention and recall, no behavioral change, and no asterixis: none, 1 point.
Total = 3 + 3 + 2 + 3 + 1 = 12.
Final answer: 12
